COM747 Week 4: Inferential Statistics and Hypothesis Testing

Lecturer demonstration notebook

Today’s question

Do female and male students get different final grades?

In student_data.csv the mean G3 is 9.97 for female and 10.91 for male students. Is that a real difference in the population of students, or could it just be sampling error? Today we learn how to decide, and how not to fool ourselves.

Learning outcomes

  1. Explain sampling error and the standard error of the mean.
  2. Calculate and interpret a confidence interval.
  3. Carry out a hypothesis test and interpret the p-value.
  4. Choose the right test: t-tests, Wilcoxon, chi-square (prop.test), ANOVA.
  5. Explain Type I and II errors, power, effect size and multiple testing.
rundata  <- read.csv("rundata.csv")
students <- read.csv("student_data.csv")

Part 1: Population versus sample

We almost never see the whole population. We see a sample and use it to infer something about the population. Different samples give different answers: sampling error.

PREDICT True mean is 50, SD 20. Will a sample of 5 give a mean close to 50? A sample of 1,000?

set.seed(4)
x5    <- rnorm(5, 50, 20);    c(mean = mean(x5), sd = sd(x5))
##     mean       sd 
## 61.18802 16.12827
x1000 <- rnorm(1000, 50, 20); c(mean = mean(x1000), sd = sd(x1000))
##     mean       sd 
## 49.27826 19.40446
set.seed(5)
x <- rnorm(2000, 50, 20)
running_mean <- cumsum(x) / seq_along(x)
plot(running_mean, type = "l", col = "#2b5fa6", lwd = 2, log = "x",
     xlab = "sample size (log scale)", ylab = "sample mean",
     main = "Law of large numbers: the sample mean settles on the true mean")
abline(h = 50, lty = 2, col = "red")

Sampling methods

Method How Risk
Simple random every member equally likely can miss small groups by chance
Stratified random within groups (e.g. campus) needs group sizes known
Convenience whoever is easy to reach bias: not representative

Part 2: Standard error and confidence intervals

\[SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]

The standard error is the SD of the sample means (the width of the CLT histogram last week). Bigger samples → smaller SE → more precise estimates.

Worked example from the lecture

Sample mean 75, SD 18, n = 36.

se <- 18 / sqrt(36); se                 # 3
## [1] 3
75 + c(-1, 1) * 1 * se                  # 68% CI: 72 to 78
## [1] 72 78
75 + c(-1, 1) * 1.96 * se               # 95% CI: 69.12 to 80.88
## [1] 69.12 80.88

Report as: 75 (95% CI 69.12 to 80.88). Margin of error = 5.88.

Small samples: use the t-distribution

qnorm(0.975)          # 1.96
## [1] 1.959964
qt(0.975, df = 14)    # 2.145 for n = 15
## [1] 2.144787
qt(0.975, df = 29)    # 2.045 for n = 30
## [1] 2.04523
x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 300)
plot(x, dnorm(x), type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "#2b5fa6", ylab = "density",
     main = "t has heavier tails than the normal when n is small")
lines(x, dt(x, df = 3),  lwd = 2, col = "#d0791a")
lines(x, dt(x, df = 14), lwd = 2, col = "#2f7d5b", lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("normal", "t, df = 3", "t, df = 14"), col = c("#2b5fa6", "#d0791a", "#2f7d5b"),
       lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 1, 2), bty = "n")

A confidence interval three ways

heights <- c(40, 42, 55, 40, 49, 46, 42, 50, 54, 44, 40, 42, 46, 48, 52, 45, 48, 44, 39, 38, 45)
n  <- length(heights)
m  <- mean(heights)
se <- sd(heights) / sqrt(n)
tc <- qt(0.975, df = n - 1)

# 1. by hand
c(lower = m - tc * se, upper = m + tc * se)
##    lower    upper 
## 42.96226 47.41869
# 2. with t.test()
t.test(heights, conf.level = 0.95)$conf.int
## [1] 42.96226 47.41869
## attr(,"conf.level")
## [1] 0.95
# 3. a reusable function
ci <- function(x, level = 0.95) {
  se <- sd(x) / sqrt(length(x)); tc <- qt(1 - (1 - level) / 2, length(x) - 1)
  c(mean = mean(x), lower = mean(x) - tc * se, upper = mean(x) + tc * se)
}
ci(heights); ci(heights, 0.99)
##     mean    lower    upper 
## 45.19048 42.96226 47.41869
##     mean    lower    upper 
## 45.19048 42.15110 48.22986

What “95% confidence” really means

set.seed(3)
true_mean <- 50
cis <- t(replicate(50, ci(rnorm(25, true_mean, 20))))
miss <- cis[, "lower"] > true_mean | cis[, "upper"] < true_mean
plot(NULL, xlim = range(cis[, 2:3]), ylim = c(1, 50), xlab = "value", ylab = "sample",
     main = paste0("50 samples, 50 95% CIs: ", sum(!miss), " contain the true mean"))
segments(cis[, "lower"], 1:50, cis[, "upper"], 1:50, col = ifelse(miss, "#d0791a", "#2b5fa6"), lwd = 2)
abline(v = true_mean, lty = 2)

If we repeated the study many times, 95% of the intervals would contain the true mean. Any single interval either does or doesn’t.

Part 3: The hypothesis-testing recipe

  1. State H0 (no difference / no effect) and H1 (there is a difference).
  2. Choose alpha, usually 0.05.
  3. Check assumptions: normality (shapiro.test), equal variances (largest/smallest variance < 1.5, or var.test).
  4. Choose and run the test → test statistic and p-value.
  5. If p < alpha, reject H0. Report the effect size and a confidence interval too.

p-value: the probability of getting a result at least this extreme if H0 were true. It is not the probability that H0 is true.

shapiro.test(students$G3)                       # not normal (the zeros)
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  students$G3
## W = 0.92873, p-value = 8.836e-13
tapply(students$G3, students$sex, var)          # 21.4 vs 20.2: ratio 1.06 < 1.5
##        F        M 
## 21.36601 20.20769
var.test(G3 ~ sex, data = students)$p.value     # no evidence of unequal variances
## [1] 0.698872

Part 4: t-tests

One-sample: is the mean first run different from 30 km?

t.test(rundata$FirstRun, mu = 30)
## 
##  One Sample t-test
## 
## data:  rundata$FirstRun
## t = -1.3158, df = 98, p-value = 0.1913
## alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 30
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  26.83873 30.64046
## sample estimates:
## mean of x 
##   28.7396

Ask: p = 0.19. What do we conclude? (We fail to reject H0. That is not the same as proving the mean is 30.)

Paired: did the same runners run further the second time?

t.test(rundata$FirstRun, rundata$SecondRun, paired = TRUE)
## 
##  Paired t-test
## 
## data:  rundata$FirstRun and rundata$SecondRun
## t = -23.986, df = 98, p-value < 2.2e-16
## alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  -5.650776 -4.787204
## sample estimates:
## mean difference 
##        -5.21899
diffs <- rundata$SecondRun - rundata$FirstRun
shapiro.test(diffs)                      # paired test assumes the differences are normal
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  diffs
## W = 0.99209, p-value = 0.8325
hist(diffs, col = "#9fd3b8", border = "white", main = "SecondRun - FirstRun", xlab = "km")

Independent (Welch): do grades differ by sex?

boxplot(G3 ~ sex, data = students, col = c("#f2c48d", "#9ab7e0"), main = "Final grade by sex")

t.test(G3 ~ sex, data = students)        # Welch by default: does not assume equal variances
## 
##  Welch Two Sample t-test
## 
## data:  G3 by sex
## t = -2.0651, df = 390.57, p-value = 0.03958
## alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group F and group M is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  -1.85073226 -0.04545244
## sample estimates:
## mean in group F mean in group M 
##        9.966346       10.914439

Non-parametric alternative: Wilcoxon / Mann–Whitney

wilcox.test(G3 ~ sex, data = students, exact = FALSE)
## 
##  Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction
## 
## data:  G3 by sex
## W = 17138, p-value = 0.04065
## alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0

Ask: p = 0.040. Significant at 0.05. But remove the 38 zeros (students who left) and run it again:

no_zeros <- students[students$G3 > 0, ]
t.test(G3 ~ sex, data = no_zeros)$p.value     # 0.053
## [1] 0.05334761

One reasonable data-cleaning decision flips the conclusion. Decide your cleaning rules before testing, report what you did, and don’t hunt for p < 0.05 (p-hacking).

Effect size: Cohen’s d

cohens_d <- function(x, y) abs(mean(x) - mean(y)) / sqrt((var(x) + var(y)) / 2)
cohens_d(students$G3[students$sex == "F"], students$G3[students$sex == "M"])   # 0.21: small
## [1] 0.2079487

Small = 0.2, medium = 0.5, large = 0.8. Statistically significant ≠ a big difference.

Part 5: Proportions, many groups, relationships

Chi-square / test of proportions (A/B testing)

25 of 30 people liked website A; 5 of 31 liked website B.

prop.test(x = c(25, 5), n = c(30, 31))
## 
##  2-sample test for equality of proportions with continuity correction
## 
## data:  c(25, 5) out of c(30, 31)
## X-squared = 24.927, df = 1, p-value = 5.955e-07
## alternative hypothesis: two.sided
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.4533774 0.8907087
## sample estimates:
##    prop 1    prop 2 
## 0.8333333 0.1612903

ANOVA: more than two groups

boxplot(G3 ~ Mjob, data = students, col = "lightsteelblue", main = "G3 by mother's job")

summary(aov(G3 ~ Mjob, data = students))
##              Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value  Pr(>F)   
## Mjob          4    307   76.66   3.754 0.00519 **
## Residuals   390   7963   20.42                   
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

ANOVA tells you some group differs, not which. Follow up with pairwise.t.test(students$G3, students$Mjob, p.adjust.method = "bonferroni").

Correlation

plot(rundata$FirstRun, rundata$SecondRun, pch = 19, col = "#2b5fa680",
     xlab = "First run (km)", ylab = "Second run (km)")
abline(lm(SecondRun ~ FirstRun, data = rundata), col = "red", lwd = 2)

cor(rundata$FirstRun, rundata$SecondRun)
## [1] 0.9762012
cor.test(rundata$FirstRun, rundata$SecondRun)
## 
##  Pearson's product-moment correlation
## 
## data:  rundata$FirstRun and rundata$SecondRun
## t = 44.333, df = 97, p-value < 2.2e-16
## alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.9647003 0.9839856
## sample estimates:
##       cor 
## 0.9762012
cor(rundata)          # which runs correlate most?
##            FirstRun SecondRun  FinalRun
## FirstRun  1.0000000 0.9762012 0.9261859
## SecondRun 0.9762012 1.0000000 0.9607919
## FinalRun  0.9261859 0.9607919 1.0000000

Part 6: Errors, power and multiple testing

H0 true H0 false
Reject H0 Type I error (false positive), probability α Correct: power = 1 − β
Don’t reject Correct Type II error (false negative), probability β

Court analogy: Type I = convicting an innocent person; Type II = acquitting a guilty one.

Power by simulation (from the lecture)

power_sim <- function(samplesize, meanX, meanY, sdX = 5, sdY = 5, studies = 1000) {
  pvalues <- replicate(studies, t.test(rnorm(samplesize, meanX, sdX), rnorm(samplesize, meanY, sdY))$p.value)
  mean(pvalues < 0.05)
}
set.seed(8)
power_sim(200, 50, 51)    # d = 0.2, n = 200: about 51%
## [1] 0.504
power_sim(500, 50, 51)    # d = 0.2, n = 500: about 88%
## [1] 0.879
power_sim(50,  50, 55)    # d = 1.0, n = 50: almost 100%
## [1] 0.999
pvalues <- replicate(1000, t.test(rnorm(200, 50, 5), rnorm(200, 51, 5))$p.value)
hist(pvalues, breaks = 20, col = "lightsteelblue", border = "white", main = "p-values from 1,000 studies (n = 200, d = 0.2)")
abline(v = 0.05, col = "red", lwd = 2)

Sample size before you collect data

power.t.test(power = 0.80, delta = 0.5, sd = 1, type = "two.sample")   # about 64 per group
## 
##      Two-sample t test power calculation 
## 
##               n = 63.76576
##           delta = 0.5
##              sd = 1
##       sig.level = 0.05
##           power = 0.8
##     alternative = two.sided
## 
## NOTE: n is number in *each* group

Multiple testing and the Bonferroni correction

set.seed(2)
# 20 tests where H0 is TRUE every time
p <- replicate(20, t.test(rnorm(30), rnorm(30))$p.value)
sum(p < 0.05)                 # "discoveries" that are false positives
## [1] 2
0.05 / 20                     # Bonferroni alpha: 0.0025
## [1] 0.0025
sum(p < 0.05 / 20)
## [1] 0
p.adjust(p, method = "bonferroni")[1:5]
## [1] 1 1 1 1 1

“If you torture the data long enough, it will confess to anything.” Pre-register your hypotheses, avoid HARKing (hypothesising after results are known), correct for multiple tests.

Choosing a test

Question Data Test in R
One mean vs a value numeric, ~normal t.test(x, mu = )
Same people measured twice paired numeric t.test(x, y, paired = TRUE) / wilcox.test(..., paired = TRUE)
Two independent groups numeric t.test(y ~ group) (Welch) / wilcox.test(y ~ group)
Three or more groups numeric aov() / kruskal.test()
Two proportions counts prop.test() / chisq.test()
Relationship two numeric cor.test() (Pearson) / cor.test(method = "spearman")
Is it normal? numeric shapiro.test()
